title: Maximum Block Sum With One Deletion

concept.title: Two states: nothing deleted yet, or one element deleted
body: Extend Kadane's algorithm. For every position keep two values for blocks that **end at this position**: `noDel`, the best sum with nothing deleted, and `oneDel`, the best sum with exactly one element deleted (the block still has to contain at least one element).

body.code:
for x in a[1:]:
    oneDel = max(oneDel + x, noDel)    # keep x after an earlier deletion, or delete x itself
    noDel  = max(noDel + x, x)          # the usual Kadane step
    best = max(best, noDel, oneDel)

body: Deleting `x` itself means the block ends just before `x` in the "no deletion" state, so `oneDel` can start from the old `noDel`. The order of the two updates matters: `oneDel` must use the *old* `noDel`.

statement: Given an array of `n` integers, choose a non-empty block of consecutive elements and you may delete at most one element from it (the block must still be non-empty after the deletion). Print the largest possible sum of the remaining elements.

examples.note: All numbers are negative: the best is a single -1.

hints: Run Kadane, but keep a second value for "one element already deleted".
To delete the current element, extend the best no-deletion block that ended just before it.
Update the deletion state with the old no-deletion value, before updating that one.

explanation: `noDel` is the usual Kadane value. `oneDel` either extends an earlier deletion by the current element or deletes the current element after the best no-deletion block that ended before it.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

noDel = best = a[0]
oneDel = -10**18
for i in range(1, n):
    x = a[i]
    oneDel = max(oneDel + x, noDel)
    noDel = max(noDel + x, x)
    best = max(best, noDel, oneDel)
print(best)
